notes.meaning: The major war to conquer Canaan was over, and the land was divided among the tribes. Joshua called the fighting men of Reuben, Gad, and eastern Manasseh together. It was finally time to release these eastern soldiers so they could return to their families.

Joshua praised these soldiers for keeping every promise they made to Moses and to him. They had pledged to cross the river armed and help their brothers conquer Canaan before settling down. They carried out that difficult duty with complete loyalty and obedience.

For about seven long years, these soldiers stayed faithfully by their fellow Israelites without deserting them. They endured years of separation from their own homes and herds. Joshua gave them full credit for keeping God's command to support their brothers until the fighting ended.

God had fulfilled His promise to give rest and peace from war to the western tribes. Because that work was finished, Joshua told the eastern soldiers they were free to go back to their own lands. Even though they longed for home, they had waited patiently until their commander officially gave the order.

Joshua gave the departing soldiers serious parting advice before they crossed the river. He urged them to take careful heed to follow the law Moses had delivered. True obedience begins with loving the Lord, and that inward love must lead to wholehearted daily devotion.

Joshua prayed for God's favor and protection over these soldiers as they prepared to march away. He knew that human effort alone could never keep them safe or faithful without God's blessing. With this warm dismissal, the troops set out for their homelands.

The writer pauses to remind the reader of how the tribe of Manasseh was split into two parts. Moses gave one half land in Bashan east of the Jordan, while Joshua gave the other half an inheritance on the west. Joshua gave a special parting blessing to the eastern half-tribe before they crossed over.

Joshua told the warriors to take their vast plunder of livestock, precious metals, and clothing back to their towns. He instructed them to share these riches with the men who had stayed behind to guard their families and lands. Those who protected the home front deserved an equal portion of the spoils of war.

The two and a half tribes officially set out from Shiloh, the central camp in Canaan where the tabernacle stood. They began their march eastward back toward the land of Gilead. They were returning to the territory God had granted them through Moses.

Near the Jordan River, the returning soldiers built a massive, eye-catching altar of stones. They did this as a visible memorial of their connection to the Lord and to their western brothers. However, because it looked like an altar for animal sacrifices, it looked like a dangerous violation of God's law.

Word traveled fast to the other tribes that the eastern soldiers had constructed a great altar along the Jordan border. To the western Israelites, this structure appeared to be an unauthorized rival to God's chosen sanctuary. They feared their brothers were already drifting into false worship.

When the western tribes heard the news, they gathered at Shiloh ready to march into battle against their own brothers. God's law strictly forbade setting up separate altars for sacrifice, and they took the threat of apostasy seriously. Their deep zeal for God made them willing to fight even their closest relatives to protect pure worship.

Before rushing blindly into war, the leaders acted with wisdom by sending a high-level delegation to find out the truth. They chose Phinehas the priest, known for his bold stand against sin in the past, along with ten top tribal leaders. This fact-finding mission showed both a deep love for God's holiness and a desire to avoid needless bloodshed.

The ambassadors crossed into Gilead and met with the leaders of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh. They delivered a formal message directly to the returned soldiers. This gave the eastern tribes an opportunity to hear the serious concerns of the rest of the nation.

Speaking for the entire congregation of the Lord, Phinehas challenged the eastern tribes with a blunt and heavy accusation. He assumed the new altar was built for sacrifices, which would be direct rebellion against God's law. He warned that setting up an independent altar was a treacherous step away from following the Lord.

Phinehas reminded them of the terrible incident at Peor, where thousands of Israelites died in a plague after worshiping a false Moabite god. Phinehas himself had stopped that plague by acting decisively for the Lord's honor. He warned that Israel was barely free from the stain of that tragedy and could not afford another disaster.

Phinehas warned that sin is never just a private matter among God's people. If the eastern tribes rebelled by worshiping at their own altar, God's anger would fall on the entire nation. The western tribes intervened quickly to protect the whole community from divine judgment.

The delegation made a remarkably generous offer to their eastern brothers. If the eastern tribes felt their land was unclean without a sacred shrine, they were invited to move across the Jordan and share the western territory. The western tribes were willing to give up some of their own property rather than watch their brothers fall into sin.

The leaders pointed to the recent story of Achan, whose secret theft brought defeat and death to many Israelite soldiers at Ai. Even though only one man sinned, the whole congregation suffered under God's wrath until the guilt was removed. If one man's hidden sin caused such grief, the open rebellion of several tribes would bring ruin on all Israel.

The leaders of the eastern tribes listened patiently to the harsh charges without interrupting or lashing out in anger. Once the delegation finished speaking, they gave a respectful and calm answer to the tribal rulers. Their humble patience helped open the way to clearing up the misunderstanding.

The eastern tribes began their defense with a powerful, repeated confession of faith in the one true God. They called upon the Lord as their supreme witness, declaring that He knew their hearts were clean of rebellion. They even stated that if they truly built the altar to revolt against God, they did not deserve to be spared.

They swore that the altar was never meant for animal sacrifices, grain offerings, or peace offerings. If they had actually intended to start their own worship rituals outside God's sanctuary, they asked the Lord Himself to punish them. They agreed completely with the principle that rival sacrificial altars were wrong.

The eastern tribes explained that deep worry, not rebellion, drove them to build the altar. They feared that because the Jordan River formed a natural dividing line, future generations in the west might disown the eastern children. If their descendants were cut off from the Lord's sanctuary, they might gradually lose their faith and stop worshiping God.

To prevent such a spiritual tragedy, the leaders decided to build a prominent structure. They stressed once more that this stone monument was never designed for burnt offerings or any other sacrifices. It was meant only as a lasting sign of belonging, not a place of worship.

The altar was designed to serve as a silent witness between both sides of the Jordan for generations to come. It would prove that the eastern tribes had every right to bring their offerings across the river to the Lord's true tabernacle. This visible symbol would protect their children from being treated as outsiders to God's covenant family.

If western Israelites ever claimed in the future that the eastern tribes had no part in God, their children could point to this monument. It was an exact copy of the bronze altar standing at the tabernacle in Shiloh. The replica proved that their ancestors shared the very same faith and worship as the rest of Israel.

The eastern tribes ended their speech with deep horror at the thought of turning against the Lord. They stated firmly that they would never build an altar for sacrifices away from the Lord's tabernacle. They fully supported the central altar as the only lawful place to present offerings to God.

When Phinehas and the ten tribal leaders heard this honest explanation, their minds were put at ease. They did not stubbornly cling to their earlier suspicions or look for reasons to stay angry. They gladly accepted their brothers' word and rejoiced that no crime had been committed.

Phinehas announced with joy that the Lord's favor and presence were clearly with Israel. Because the eastern tribes had remained faithful, the whole nation was saved from the dreadful disaster of God's wrath and a bloody civil war. Preventing sin and judgment was seen as a wonderful act of rescue for all Israel.

Phinehas and the delegation traveled back across the Jordan to Canaan to deliver their report. They told the waiting congregation everything the eastern tribes had explained. The leaders gave an honest and favorable account of their meeting in Gilead.

The news brought great relief and happiness to the gathered Israelites, and they praised God for keeping their brothers faithful. All plans for war were immediately dropped. What could have been a catastrophic conflict ended instead in peace and thanksgiving.

The eastern tribes named the altar "Witness," which is what the Hebrew word Ed means. This name served as a permanent reminder to both sides of the river that the Lord alone is the true God. The monument stood as a pledge of lasting unity and pure faith across the Jordan divide.
